title: Topology-aware kernel placement & KV-coherence for multi-GPU serving (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This doc proposes a topology-aware approach for placing compute kernels and KV-cache shards across multiple GPUs in a single node and across nodes. The goal is to reduce tail latency and cross-device bandwidth contention while preserving KV coherence during resharding and scale events. This is intentionally a practical draft: heuristics + small runtime changes that we can prototype in the next sprint.

Context and motivation:
- We already use sharded KV caches and tensor/pipeline parallelism. Current placement is largely round-robin or static assignment based on layer index; this ignores machine topology (NVLink groups, PCIe lanes, NIC proximity) and leads to bursts of cross-link traffic and NCCL congestion at certain sequence lengths.
- Observed symptoms in staging: periodic p95 spikes when long-context chat requests hit layers whose KV shards live on a distant NVLink domain; NCCL bandwidth saturation for all-to-all KV syncs during rollouts.

Design goals (high level):
1) Minimize high-latency cross-domain transfers for hot KV hits and heavy matmul kernels.
2) Maintain strong-enough KV coherence for correctness during inference and live resharding with minimal synchronization overhead.
3) Be topology-aware (NVLink cliques, PCIe-only GPUs, multi-socket NUMA) but remain lightweight to avoid long scheduling decisions.
4) Provide safe fallback paths and deterministic behavior for debugging/repro.

Core ideas / proposal:
A. Topology model & discovery
- At startup the agent queries local topology: GPU ids, NVLink adjacency matrix (via nvidia-smi topo --matrix or NVML), PCIe switch grouping, and NIC adjacency.
- The runtime constructs "domains": intra-node NVLink cliques (fast), inter-domain crosslink (slower), remote node (slowest). Assign a domain id to each GPU.

B. Kernel placement heuristic (layer -> domain mapping)
- For each layer we estimate three signals: compute intensity (FLOPs / token), KV dependency weight (how many KV reads/writes per token), and memory working set (KV size touched).
- Heuristic: co-locate a layer on a GPU in the same domain as its primary KV shard if KV weight > threshold. For layers with heavy compute but light KV, prefer GPUs with highest local compute headroom.
- For pipeline/tensor parallelism combinations: bind tensor-parallel partitions of the same transformer layer within the same domain when possible to maximize local all-reduce bandwidth (reduce NCCL across domains). Pipeline stage boundaries remain a placement unit if stage's KV locality differs significantly.

C. KV shard placement & coherence
- Shard primary: Each KV shard has a single primary GPU (owner) and optionally read-replicas in the same domain. The primary handles writes (evictions, append on generation).
- Replication: lightweight in-domain replication (one replica per NVLink sibling) using best-effort async replication for hot keys (write-through but async confirmation).
- Coherence protocol: epoch-based sequence numbers per shard plus a small invalidation log. Readers check sequence before using cached local replica; if mismatch, they fetch from primary.
- Resharding: when reassigning primaries (scale up/down or rollout), move primaries within the same domain first. Global cross-domain reshards use a two-phase handoff: mark new primary, allow short draining window for old writes, then switch epoch. This limits global sync spikes.

D. NCCL tuning and topology-aware collectives
- Strategy: choose collective algorithm per-communication-pattern and per-domain topology.
- Intra-domain (NVLink clique): prefer high-performance LL/LL128-like algorithms when available, or set NCCL_ALGO=ring with optimized chunk sizes for large tensors.
- Cross-domain (PCIe/NIC): use tree or hierarchical algorithms, increasing chunk sizes to reduce per-call overhead. For small messages prefer a dedicated point-to-point pipeline to avoid NCCL oversubscription.
- Environment knobs: expose runtime tuning flags (examples):
  * REDWOOD_COMM_INTRA_ALGO=ll128
  * REDWOOD_COMM_INTER_ALGO=tree
  * REDWOOD_COMM_CHUNK_BYTES=1048576
  * REDWOOD_KV_REPLICA_WINDOW_MS=50
- Runtime will monitor bandwidth counters and automatically shift algorithms if cross-domain saturation detected (fallback from ll128 to ring-tree hybrid).

E. Scheduler changes (fast, local decisions)
- We extend the existing scheduler with a "topology score" computed for each placement option: topology_score = alpha * locality_score + beta * compute_headroom + gamma * estimated_comm_cost. Default weights tuned to prioritize locality for latency-sensitive routes.
- Scheduling path is time-bounded (e.g., max 500us additional decision time) to avoid adding latency to critical requests. If decision times out, fall back to previous static assignment.

F. Fallbacks and safety
- If topology discovery fails, use conservative default (no cross-node replication, single-shard primaries).
- On network anomalies detected by NCCL (timeouts, rank failures), switch to read-through mode where KV reads pull directly from primary over RDMA with backpressure to avoid thundering-herd.
- Maintain debug flags to force single-domain placement for repro.

Micro configs & example (draft):
- Shard config snippet (YAML-like just for human reading):
  shard-512k:
    primary_hint: domain0
    replica_domains: [domain0]
    replica_policy: async-in-domain
    write_mode: primary-only

- Runtime env example:
  REDWOOD_COMM_HEURISTICS=topology_aware
  REDWOOD_MAX_PLACEMENT_MS=0.5
  REDWOOD_KV_EPOCH_TIMEOUT_MS=10

Observability and metrics to add:
- Per-shard metrics: p50/p95 KV read latency, local-hit-rate, replica-staleness histogram (epoch differences), cross-domain bytes/sec.
- Per-domain NCCL metrics: active_streams, bytes/sec, retries/timeouts.
- Placement metrics: decisions_count, decisions_timeout_rate, topology_score distribution.
- Experiment hooks: enable side-by-side comparison route to record both old placement and new placement decisions for identical inputs to evaluate delta in latency and bandwidth.

Rollout plan (minimal safe path):
1) Implement topology discovery agent + metrics only behind flag. Run in canary to validate domain detection.
2) Add read-only replica logic: create per-domain replica caches but do not use them by default (metrics only).
3) Enable topology-aware placement for a small set of low-traffic models (A/B test). Collect p50/p95, KV hit-rate, NCCL counters.
4) Enable write-through replica mode for in-domain replicas. Monitor correctness and epoch mismatches.
5) Gradually expand to more models, tune weights, and add automatic NCCL algorithm switching.

Tests & experiments (concrete):
- Microbench: synthetic KV microbench that hits a variable skewed key distribution; measure p50/p95 with and without topology-aware placement and with different replica counts.
- End-to-end: long-context chat workload on a 2-node heterogeneous cluster (1 NVLink-clique + 1 PCIe-only GPU); compare p95 and NCCL bandwidth under 1x, 3x, 10x request pressure.
- Failure injection: simulate GPU removal and force reshard; assert no data loss and bounded latency spike (< 2x baseline p95).

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How many in-domain replicas are worth the write amplification? For hot-key heavy workloads, extra in-domain replicas reduce latency but increase write traffic. We should quantify threshold by percent of requests that are hot.
- Interaction with tensor-parallel kernels that require synchronized all-reduce: colocating TP ranks reduces cross-domain collectives but may worsen load-balancing across GPUs if compute skew exists. What automated placement policy balances both?
- How to efficiently support multi-tenant nodes where tenants own GPUs: limit topology-aware placement to tenant-owned GPUs versus shared pools.

Action items / next steps:
- [Priya] Prototype topology discovery + domain modeling (1 sprint).
- [Jordan] Implement epoch-based KV sequence numbers and local replica check logic (1 sprint).
- [Luis] Add NCCL algorithm switcher and simple bandwidth health monitor (1 sprint).
- [Maya] Design experiment harness and dashboards for per-shard metrics (1 sprint).

Appendix: quick glossary
- domain: a group of GPUs with fast interconnect (e.g., NVLink clique).
- primary: the owner of a KV shard that applies writes.
- replica: a local copy of a shard kept for read locality; may be async.
- epoch: monotonically increasing number attached to shard state to detect staleness.

Notes:
- This doc intentionally avoids prescribing a fully-consistent distributed cache; we accept eventual consistency within small bounded windows to keep write latencies low.
- Implementation should be modular: the placement heuristic should be separate from the KV store so we can iterate independently.
